title: Where you're from, work and languages
goal: Talk about where you're from, what you do and which languages you speak — while picking up the layer of Malaysian vocabulary borrowed from English.
bekal: name jobs and workplaces with the right Malaysian words
recognize the English borrowing patterns that let you read hundreds of words on sight
use *buat apa*, *kat* and *nak* — three of the most common conversational words in Malaysia

dialogs.title: Dialogue — In the college cafeteria
dialogs.intro: Afternoon in the college cafeteria. Sarah is sitting alone with a plate of nasi lemak when Haziq comes over with his tray and asks if he can sit down.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Saya Haziq. Awak buat apa kat sini? Belajar ke, kerja?
lines.id: I'm Haziq. What are you doing here? Studying or working?
lines.literal: I Haziq. you do what at here? study [question], work?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya belajar. Ambil jurusan Sains Komputer.
lines.id: I'm studying. I'm doing Computer Science.
lines.literal: I study. take major Science Computer.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tahun satu. Baru mula. Awak pula?
lines.id: First year. Just started. And you?
lines.literal: year one. just start. you in-turn?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Saya tahun tiga, Kejuruteraan Awam. Ayah saya jurutera juga.
lines.id: I'm in third year, Civil Engineering. My dad's an engineer too.
lines.literal: I year three, engineering civil. father I engineer also.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Mak saya cikgu. Dia mengajar kat sekolah menengah.
lines.id: My mum's a teacher. She teaches at a secondary school.
lines.literal: mum I teacher. she teach at school middle.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ayah saya doktor gigi, mak saya kakitangan bank.
lines.id: My dad's a dentist, and my mum works at a bank.
lines.literal: father I doctor tooth, mum I staff bank.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Awak cakap Melayu elok juga. Belajar kat mana?
lines.id: Your Malay is pretty good. Where did you learn it?
lines.literal: you speak Malay fine also. learn at where?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tak belajar pun — hampir sama dengan bahasa saya. Cuma perkataan je yang lain.
lines.id: I didn't really learn it — it's almost the same as my language. Only the words are different.
lines.literal: not learn even — almost same with language I. only word just that different.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Betul tu. Nanti saya ajar awak perkataan orang sini.
lines.id: That's true. I'll teach you the local words later.
lines.literal: right that. later I teach you word person here.

notes: **Kat** is the conversational form of **di** (at, in) — short for *dekat* (near). *Kat sini* = here, *kat rumah* = at home, *kat mana?* = where? It turns up in almost every spoken sentence in Malaysia (Indonesian doesn't use it at all). In formal writing it is still written *di*.
**Buat apa** means **what are you doing / what are you up to** — not "make what". *Awak buat apa?* = "What are you doing?" *Buat* also means **for**: *Ini buat awak* = "This is for you".

**Cikgu** = teacher. It's shortened from *encik guru* ("Mr Teacher") and is used both as a job title and as a form of address: *Cikgu, boleh tanya?* ("Teacher, may I ask something?"). **Sekolah menengah** = secondary school (ages 13–17); **sekolah rendah** = primary school.
**Kakitangan** means **staff, employees** — literally "feet and hands". It's the official word you'll see on notices: *Kakitangan sahaja* = "Staff only". ⚠️ In Indonesian it means "accomplice".
**Elok** means **good, nice, fine** and is very common. *Elok juga* = "pretty good". Its cousins: *cantik* (pretty, for things and people), *bagus*, *hebat* (great).

grammars.title: English loanwords: a pattern that unlocks hundreds of words
body: Malay was shaped by about a century and a half of British rule, and it borrowed thousands of English words, respelling them the Malay way. Learn the patterns and you can guess words you've never heard. (Indonesian, shaped by the Dutch, often borrowed the same words from Dutch instead — one big reason the two vocabularies differ.)
after: The spelling follows the Malay *sound*: *kaunter* because Malay *au* sounds like "ow" in *count*; *-syen* because *sy* is "sh". Some words also take a different road from English: an office is *pejabat*, not "ofis" (though *ofis* is heard too); a ticket is *tiket*; a bank account is *akaun*.

⚠️ Two traps in this table: **kolej** often means a **student residence** (a residential college), while the campus itself is *kampus*. And **doktor** means a medical **doctor**; a PhD is *Doktor Falsafah (PhD)*.

blocks.text: You can say *Saya bekerja sebagai…* (I work as…), *Saya seorang…* (I'm a…), or leave out the verb altogether (*Ayah saya doktor* = my father [is a] doctor). Malay has no word for "a" or "is" here. What you need to learn is the words:

head: Malay
English
Note
rows: *Cikgu* in speech and as a title.

blocks.text: The word **juru** (expert, skilled person) builds many job titles in Malay: *jurutera* (engineer), *jururawat* (nurse), *juruterbang* (pilot), *jurugambar* (photographer), *jurulatih* (coach), *juruaudit* (auditor), *jurubahasa* (interpreter). If you meet a new word starting with *juru-*, the guess is almost always "someone skilled at X".
Simpler than English: country names take a capital letter, a language is *bahasa* + name, and a nationality is *orang* (person) + name — no separate adjectives to learn.

Two spellings to watch: **Jepun** (Japan) and **Inggeris** (English, with an extra *e*). Both appear constantly in Malaysian writing. If you've met Indonesian, note that it spells them *Jepang* and *Inggris* — mixing them up gives you away at once.

In Malaysia, the words **bangsa** (race, nation) and **kaum** (community, ethnic group) are used for the country's ethnic groups: *orang Melayu*, *orang Cina*, *orang India*, *kaum Iban*, *kaum Kadazan*. This is ordinary everyday usage with no negative undertone. Note also that **orang Melayu** (ethnic Malays) is not the same as **orang Malaysia** (Malaysian citizens); mixing them up is a mistake people notice quickly.

blocks.title: Asking back
items: **Awak buat apa kat sini?** — What are you doing here?
**Awak kerja apa?** — What do you do (for work)?
**Awak belajar apa?** — What are you studying?
**Awak orang mana?** — Where are you from? (home region)
**Awak duduk kat mana?** — Where do you live? (⚠️ *duduk* = to sit, but also to live somewhere)
